title: 5 Quick and Easy Ways to Earn Respect As a Leader
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain opens with a story from his first leadership role, when he committed his team to an unrealistic timeline to appear flawless, then owned the mistake to his manager and team and was met with support rather than scorn. The lesson he draws is that respect comes not from perfection but from being authentic, accountable, and human. He develops five practices: be yourself, listen rather than merely hear, be consistent, show you care, and give credit where it is due. Each is illustrated with a workplace anecdote, such as thanking a team member for exposing a gap in his plan, starting meetings on time even when his boss was late, and granting a burned-out employee time off. Each section ends with an actionable tip, and the piece closes by arguing that respect is earned slowly but can be lost quickly through a single misstep.
points: Owning a public mistake, an unrealistic timeline committed without consulting the team, earned Jain respect rather than contempt.
Acknowledging an overlooked gap a team member raised in a review meeting made others feel safe to speak up about issues.
Starting meetings on time regardless of who was late, even senior leaders, set a tone of accountability that spread beyond meetings.
Reflective listening, paraphrasing before responding, is offered as the practical tool for making people feel heard.
Publicly crediting individual contributions before senior leadership costs nothing but pays back in loyalty and respect.
quotes: I then called a meeting with my team, acknowledged what I had done and that it was wrong, and asked for their feedback on how we could move forward together. I did this with authenticity and with genuine concern. I could literally feel my heart pounding, but I was feeling an eerie sense of relaxation for having done the right thing.

It was amazing to see how this moment of vulnerability shifted the atmosphere in the room—it empowered others to speak up about potential issues without fear of being judged. What could have been a stressful debate became a collaborative session where everyone felt valued.
I love that quote by Andy Stanley because it is so true. If you don’t listen, those who have genuine inputs will eventually stop speaking up and even leave.
At first, this simple rule seemed insignificant. But over time, it set the tone for accountability across the team — beyond just the meetings.

People knew that I valued their time and that they could count on me to keep my word. Similarly, I made sure to follow up on commitments, even when priorities shifted. This consistency created a culture of accountability in my team, and a mutual respect for each others’ time.

Leaders who acknowledge the contributions of others create an environment where respect flows both ways. On the other hand, leaders who take credit for their team’s work risk losing trust and credibility.
And it takes time and effort to earn respect. On the flip side, a single misstep can cause you to slip and lose your team’s respect very quickly.
